predecessors.name: Byzantine Empire
predecessors.text: Constantinople and Thrace, taken in the sack of April 1204; the emperor's quarter under the Partitio Romaniae (late September/October 1204)

successors.name: Empire of Nicaea
successors.text: Constantinople, taken by Alexios Strategopoulos on the night of 24/25 July 1261

successors.name: Empire of Nicaea
successors.text: the Latin lands in Asia Minor: the Bithynian coast, Nicomedia, Pegai, Cyzicus, the Troad and Mysia up to Kalamos

successors.name: Despotate of Epirus
successors.text: western and inland Thrace: Adrianople, Didymoteicho, Mosynopolis and the lower Maritsa

successors.name: Second Bulgarian Empire
successors.text: Philippopolis with the Rhodopes and the Melnik valley: the Latin duchy of Philippopolis (Renier of Trit) and Alexius Slav's Rhodope lordship

ledger.x: Sack of 12-13 April 1204; Baldwin of Flanders elected 9 May and 'crowned on 16 May in the Hagia Sophia'; Partitio Romaniae late September/October 1204 (one quarter to the emperor, three eighths to Venice, three eighths to the barons).
1204: the Kingdom of Thessalonica is 'established as a vassal of the Latin Empire'.
Latin invasion of Bithynia: Theodore Laskaris 'routed... at Poemanenum on 6 December' 1204; Adramyttion 19 March 1205; 'most of Bithynia' Latin by spring 1205.
'Latins captured most of Bithynia by 1205 after defeating Theodore I Laskaris at Poemanenum and Prusa'.
After Adrianople Henry recalled the Asian army; Theodore 'expelled the Latin garrisons from most Anatolian fortresses'.
Thracian revolt, spring 1205; Battle of Adrianople 14 April 1205 ('Bulgarian victory'), Baldwin I captured; 'During the course of 1205, Kaloyan captured Serres and Philippopolis'.

Adrianople itself stayed in Greek-Latin hands ('The Bulgarians besieged Adrianople twice, but failed to take the city'); Didymoteicho fell after 31 January 1206; Herakleia and Tzurulum ravaged, Rodosto evacuated.

David Komnenos chose 'to prefer a nominal Latin suzerainty to annexation by the Nicaean emperor' and asked Henry 'to treat his land as Latin territory' (1205/06); the relation lapsed with his lands (Nicaean by 1212-14).
'The Latins invaded Asia Minor and captured Nicomedia and Cyzicus during the winter of 1206-1207.'
Two-year truce of 1207 'authorizing Theodore to destroy two fortifications at Nicomedia and Cyzicus'; Thierry de Loos captured.
'A truce was signed with Theodore, newly proclaimed Emperor of Nicaea' (1207).
Beroia (1207/08) then Henry 'managed to defeat him in the Battle of Philippopolis (1208)'; Henry 'reclaim[ed] most of the lost territories in Thrace until 1210'.
Alexius Slav, Kaloyan's nephew, did homage to Henry (1208/09) and married his daughter; the 1210-1219 shape's northern lobe corresponds to his lands.
Parliament of Ravennika (May 1209): under Geoffrey I 'the Principality of Achaea became the direct vassal of the Latin Empire of Constantinople' instead of Thessalonica's.
Otto de la Roche did homage to Henry at Ravennika 1209; after Thessalonica's fall 'Athens itself was independent of any other sovereign than the Latin emperor'.
Ravano dalle Carceri recognised Venetian overlordship in March 1209 and did homage to Henry in May 1209.
Marco Sanudo did homage to Henry in 1210.
'In 1210 a peace was concluded, when the Hungarians and Latin empire made an alliance'; Henry's marriage to Maria of Bulgaria arranged 1213.
Rhyndacus, 15 October 1211: Henry 'routed Theodore's troops' and marched unopposed to Nymphaion.

'The Latins also seized some strategically important Bithynian fortresses'; the Treaty of Nymphaeum (December 1214) 'recognized their control of most of Bithynia and Mysia' with Kalamos as the uninhabited boundary village.
David died 13 December 1212; Laskaris 'eventually captured Heraclea Pontica and Amastris' and the Treaty of Nymphaeum omits him.
Treaty of Nymphaeum, December 1214 (Treadgold proposes 1212).
Robert backed the Laskaris brothers against Vatatzes; Poimanenon 'early 1224 (or possibly late 1223)'.
'Robert's first loss was Thessalonica in 1224 to Theodore Doukas of Epirus' (December 1224); conqueror in note: despotate-of-epirus.

Peace of 1225 after Poimanenon ('early 1224 (or possibly late 1223)'): 'the Latins abandoned all their Asian possessions except for the eastern shore of the Bosporus' and 'the city of Nicomedia with the surrounding region'.
'John III's victory led to territorial concessions by the Latin Empire in 1225.'
Vatatzes' 'seizure of Adrianople' after the 1225 concessions; Theodore of Epirus 'drove the Nicaean garrison out of Adrianople and annexed much of Thrace in 1227'.
'Epirote armies then conquered Thrace in 1225-26, appearing before Constantinople itself.'
1225-26: 'Epirote armies then conquered Thrace in 1225–26, appearing before Constantinople itself'; the towns of the polygon are my reading.
'a truce was concluded in 1228'.
After Klokotnitsa (9 March 1230) Ivan Asen II took Thrace; the Latin duchy of Philippopolis lapsed about 1230 and Alexius Slav joined Bulgaria.
Conqueror in note: second-bulgarian-empire.
Spring 1235: Vatatzes 'crossed the Dardanelles and took over Gallipoli' and seized Latin Thrace 'from the east coast up to the mouth of the Marica', 'including the fortress of Tzurulum'.
'In 1235, finally, the last Latin possessions fell to Nicaea' (the Nicomedia region).
Joint Bulgarian-Nicaean siege of Constantinople 1235 - spring 1236 ('Latin victory'); Venice, Genoa, Pisa and Geoffrey II of Achaea relieved the city.
Constantinople and its immediate environs to Selymbria.
Siege abandoned in spring 1236; Ivan Asen II changed sides.
Constantinople and its immediate environs to Selymbria.
'By 1247, the Nicaeans had effectively surrounded the main holdings of the Emperor'; Tzurulum, retaken by Bulgaria after 1235 and Latin again, fell to Vatatzes in 1247.
Baldwin II transferred the suzerainty to William II of Achaea (1248).
Michael VIII's failed gate plot and 'unsuccessful assault on Galata' (1260); alliance with Genoa March 1261.
Night of 24/25 July 1261: Alexios Strategopoulos' 800 men entered the city; Baldwin II 'fled the city by ship'; Michael VIII entered on 15 August.
Constantinople and its immediate environs to Selymbria.
The suzerainty survived on paper with the exiled emperor and was transferred to Charles of Anjou at Viterbo (24/27 May 1267).
the Duchy of Athens.
Venice was the triarchs' effective overlord.
'The last Latin emperor, Baldwin II, went into exile, but the imperial title survived' (Baldwin II to 1273, Philip of Courtenay, Catherine of Courtenay, Catherine of Valois).

wars.name: Latin-Nicaean war of 1204-1207
wars.outcome: Poimanenon (6 December 1204) and Adramyttion (19 March 1205) Latin victories undone after Adrianople; Nicomedia and Cyzicus 1206-07; truce 1207

wars.name: Bulgarian-Latin war of 1205-1210
wars.outcome: Adrianople 14 April 1205 (Bulgarian victory, Baldwin I captured); Serres and Philippopolis Bulgarian 1205; Henry's recovery 1206-08 (Beroia, Philippopolis 1208); peace 1210

wars.name: Latin-Nicaean war of 1211-1214
wars.outcome: Rhyndacus 15 October 1211; Treaty of Nymphaeum December 1214: Bithynian coast and Mysia to Kalamos Latin

wars.name: Poimanenon war
wars.outcome: Nicaean victory at Poimanenon (1223/24); 1225 peace: all Asia but Nicomedia ceded; Vatatzes took Adrianople and the islands

wars.name: Epirote conquest of Thrace
wars.outcome: Theodore Komnenos Doukas took Adrianople (1227) and Thrace to the walls of Constantinople; truce 1228

wars.name: Siege of Constantinople (1235-1236)
wars.outcome: Latin victory in the siege; Nicaea kept Gallipoli, Tzurulum and the Thracian coast to the Maritsa

wars.name: Reconquest of Constantinople
wars.outcome: Nicaean victory, 25 July 1261; end of the Latin Empire

certainty.note: A feudal empire of fiefs and vassal states; the direct domain in Thrace and Asia shifted with every campaign and the Cliopatria shapes lag the losses by a decade or more.
